title: Reading Together: Start at Birth
hook: You don't need to wait until your child can follow a story. Reading aloud from birth builds language, attention, and your bond — and even a few interactive minutes a day counts.
key_points: Read together daily, starting at birth — the earlier you begin, the stronger early language tends to be.
Shared reading builds language and literacy, supports brain development, and deepens your bond.
Make it interactive: point, name things, ask questions, and let your child turn the pages.
A few minutes counts; print books beat screens because they invite back-and-forth with you.
content_html: Reading with your child isn't something to save for when they can sit still and follow a plot. The AAP encourages shared reading starting at birth, and research finds that the earlier parents begin reading aloud, the stronger a child's language skills tend to be by preschool. Beyond words, those moments in your lap link books with security, your voice, and connection.
extra_html: What makes it powerful is the back-and-forth, not getting through every page. Make it interactive — point at the pictures, name what you see, ask simple questions, and let your child turn the pages. This dialogic style is the approach behind programs like Reach Out and Read, which the AAP supports. Print books work better than screens here because they invite that shared, responsive exchange, and even a few minutes a day counts. This is general educational information from the AAP — your pediatrician can suggest books and tips suited to your child's stage.

source.name: HealthyChildren.org (AAP) — Shared Reading Starting at Birth Offers Lifelong Benefits

related.title: Serve and Return: Talking Builds the Brain
related.hook: Every time you answer your baby's coo, babble, or gesture, you're building their brain. These back-and-forth 'serve and return' moments are the engine of early language — and they're free.

related.title: The Toddler Language Explosion
related.hook: Somewhere in the second year, many toddlers go from a handful of words to picking up new ones almost daily — and talking with them is what fuels it.

related.title: What Play Looks Like at Each Age
related.hook: Play is a child's real work — and it changes shape as they grow, from staring at your face to elaborate make-believe. The best 'toy' is usually a tuned-in grown-up, not a gadget.
